covering.note: Its fur is long and silky.

size.note: It is one of the biggest living lemurs, weighing up to about 10 kg.

diet.note: It mostly eats young leaves, plus flowers, fruit, seeds and bark.

activity.note: It is thought to be the most daytime-active of all lemurs.

social.note: A family group is a mated pair and up to four of their young.

young.note: A mother has one baby every 2 or 3 years.

clues.text: Its tail is just a tiny stub, only about 5 cm long.
Its silky fur is mostly black with white patches, and its tufted ears are black.
It clings upright to tree trunks and travels by leaping from trunk to trunk.
On the ground it hops upright on its back legs, holding its arms above its head.
Families sing loud, wailing songs that can be heard up to 2 km away.
Each family keeps its own territory and settles most border meetings by singing, not fighting.
Young, tender leaves are its main food.
A baby clings to its mother's belly, then rides on her back from about 4 or 5 months old.
Forest cleared for slash-and-burn farming, logging and firewood is its main threat.

facts.text: In 2021 scientists found that indri songs use the same kinds of rhythm as human music. It was the first mammal besides people known to do this.
No zoo has ever kept indris for long, so saving its rainforest is the only way to save it.
Its Malagasy name, babakoto, is often translated as 'father' or 'ancestor'. Many local legends treat it as sacred.
The adult female is the boss of the family group.
In the morning it often sits facing the rising sun, as if sunbathing.
It sometimes climbs down to eat soil, which may help it handle harsh chemicals in the seeds it eats.
Young indris move around on their own at 8 months, but stay close to their mother until they are 2.
Its numbers are thought to be falling by 80% or more over 33 years, from forest loss and hunting.
It is hunted for meat, even in places where old taboos once protected it.
Scientists expect climate change alone to shrink its range by about 40% between 2000 and 2080.
